big: Two friends invest on the same day. One looks at her fund every morning and panics at each dip. The other checks once a year. Same fund, very different experience.

lines: My fund is down 8% this month. Should I sell before it falls more?
First, when do you need this money? Let us look at how three kinds of funds typically move over time.

alt: Three lines: equity rises most but dips deepest, debt rises slowest and steadiest
caps: Equity grows the most over the long run, but it dips the deepest.
Hybrid sits in the middle, dipping less and growing less.
Debt is the smoothest, and grows the slowest in this made-up path.
Made-up paths, not forecasts. The shape is the lesson: more growth, more swing.

intro: Every fund carries a label showing how risky its holdings are.
rows: Very steady, such as short-term debt
Balanced mixes of shares and bonds
note: The label is set by the fund's holdings. Pick one you could sit through when it falls.

q: Meena's equity fund is down 8% and she needs the money in 8 years. What is the sound approach?
opts: Sell now, since a fall that has started always keeps going
Check the goal and time frame still stand, and stay invested if so
Switch everything into the fund that gained most last month
Stop looking at the fund until the loss has been fully recovered
why: Falls do not always continue. Selling after one locks in a loss with years left to recover.
With 8 years left and no change in plan, a dip is part of the ride, so review the goal and stay.
Chasing last month's winner often means buying high, and it ignores the goal and risk.
Avoiding the statement does not help. A calm review of the plan is better than looking away.

q: Rohan can sleep through falls and has 15 years to go. Meena panics at a 5% dip and needs the money in 3 years. What do they need?
opts: The same fund, since both want good returns from their savings
Meena should hold more shares, since she needs the money sooner
Neither needs to look at the riskometer if the fund is well known
Rohan can hold a higher-risk fund, while Meena needs a steadier one
why: Different time frames and comfort levels mean different funds suit them. Return alone is not the test.
Needing money soon argues for less risk, not more. A fall near the goal date is harder to recover.
A well-known name does not change the risk. The riskometer is how you check a fund's swings.
Rohan's long horizon and calm temperament fit more risk, and Meena's short horizon needs steadiness.

q: Which best describes how diversification helps?
opts: It guarantees that your fund will never lose money in any year
It increases the return by concentrating money in the best company
It spreads money across many holdings so one bad one cannot sink it
It removes the need to think about how long you can stay invested
why: Diversification lowers the damage of single failures. It does not make a fund fall-proof.
Concentrating money in one company is the opposite of spreading it.
Many holdings mean one failure takes only a small bite out of the whole pool.
Diversification does not replace thinking about the time you have for the goal.

q: A fund gained 30% one year and lost 12% the next. What does this show about it?
opts: It is volatile: big swings are normal for equity, so judge it over years
The fund is broken, since good funds do not lose money in any year
The manager was wrong, since a skilled one avoids all losses
It must be a debt fund, because only debt funds move this way
why: Big swings describe volatility. Judge it over years that match your goal, not one year.
Equity funds can lose money in a year, even good ones. A single bad year does not prove a broken fund.
No manager avoids every loss. A single down year says little about skill.
Equity funds typically swing like this. Debt funds move far less in most years.

pts: More possible growth always comes with bigger swings.
Check the riskometer against the amount of fall you could sit through.
Time and diversification reduce the damage of falls, but do not remove them.
